content.text:
ADBE’s 2026-03-11 to 2026-03-13 move looks like one coherent, company-specific selloff centered on Adobe’s post-close March 12 earnings/CEO-transition package, rather than three unrelated daily moves: the stock slipped 0.52% on March 11 to $273.71, fell 1.43% on March 12 to $269.78, then dropped 7.58% on March 13 to $249.32, matching the -8.91% rolling signal from March 11 to March 13 [1]. The fundamental print itself was not weak—Adobe reported record Q1 FY2026 revenue of $6.40 billion, 12% year-over-year growth, non-GAAP EPS of $6.06, subscription revenue growth of 13%, and Q2 revenue guidance of $6.43 billion to $6.48 billion while reaffirming FY2026 targets [2]. The problem was that the same release announced CEO Shantanu Narayen would transition out after a successor is named, while remaining chair, which introduced succession uncertainty at the same time investors were already debating Adobe’s AI strategy [2].

That firm-specific interpretation is well supported by contemporaneous coverage and analyst reaction. Reuters reported that Adobe shares fell more than 7% in extended trading after the CEO transition news, tying the move to renewed concern about Adobe’s strategy amid AI disruption and noting competitive pressure from AI-enabled design tools from rivals such as Canva and Figma [3]. Barclays then downgraded Adobe to Equal Weight from Overweight and cut its price target to $275 from $335, citing near-term revenue-growth concerns, leadership transition risk, weaker net-new ARR versus estimates, and generative-AI pressure on Adobe Stock sales as users create images with text prompts rather than buying stock images [4]. A same-day DOJ action added another company-specific overhang: on March 13 the Justice Department announced a proposed stipulated order requiring $75 million in civil penalties and $75 million in free services to resolve alleged violations of online-subscription disclosure and cancellation rules [5]. Because ADBE opened March 13 at $249.00 versus the prior $269.78 close, most of the decline had already occurred before the DOJ news flow could be fully digested, so the settlement looks like an incremental reputational/regulatory weight rather than the dominant trigger [1][5].

The industry and macro evidence is present but secondary, which broadly fits the attribution’s emphasis on firm-specific drivers. The software tape was soft—IGV fell 0.87% on March 12 and 0.94% on March 13, from $85.74 on March 11 to $84.19 on March 13—and Reuters’ Adobe story explicitly framed the stock reaction against investor worries about AI disruption in design software [3][6]. However, the provided factor model says the industry contribution was -15% of the negative episode return, i.e., an offset rather than a drag, which does not neatly line up with IGV’s modest decline; that discrepancy should be treated as a regression-specific exposure/sign issue rather than a clean public-news narrative [6]. Macro was a modest additional headwind: AP reported that on March 13 the S&P 500 fell 0.6%, the Nasdaq dropped 0.9%, and oil moved back above $100 as Iran-war fallout raised inflation pressure, consistent with a smaller market drag versus the much larger Adobe-specific shock [7].
